I traced each call site against its pre-diff counterpart:

- `unquote()` still runs before the path-safety guard in every case (comment at line 91 even calls this out explicitly) — preserves the original ordering that matters for traversal payloads double-encoded to slip past a pre-unquote check.
- `guard=True` is passed only for EXTRACT, DELETE_LOCAL, DELETE_REMOTE — exactly the three actions that called `_check_path_safe` before the refactor. QUEUE and STOP still skip the guard, identical to pre-diff behavior.
- I verified in `src/python/controller/controller.py` (lines 1099–1134) that QUEUE/STOP resolve `file_name` via `self.__model.get_file(command.filename)` — a model/name lookup, not a filesystem path join — so the absent guard on those two was never a traversal sink; it's unchanged, non-regressive behavior either way.
- Response shapes, timeout handling, and success/error message formatting are byte-for-byte identical to the originals, just parameterized via `success_msg.format(file_name)`.

No injection, auth, secrets, data-exposure, or path-traversal regressions were introduced by this refactor. The bulk-command path (`__handle_bulk_command` / `_process_bulk_commands`), which has its own independent `_check_path_safe` call per guarded action, is untouched by this diff.

agent_notes: Scope: a pure refactor inside one file, src/python/web/handler/controller.py. Five single-action handlers (queue, stop, extract, delete_local, delete_remote) now delegate to a new method, _dispatch_command (lines 76-105). Routes, HTTP verbs, URL patterns and handler method names in add_routes (lines 66-70) are unchanged, so the web_app_builder.py wiring and the frontend REST contract are unaffected.

Path-safety guard: no loosening. Before the diff, only extract, delete_local and delete_remote called _check_path_safe. After the diff, exactly those three pass guard=True (lines 123-144), and queue/stop still pass no guard, as before. The order is also unchanged: unquote runs first (line 91), then the guard (lines 93-96), then the command is queued. So a double-encoded traversal such as %252e%252e%252f is still decoded before the check. The bulk path calls _check_path_safe directly (line 338) and is not touched by this diff.

Response shapes are the same. The timeout still returns 504 with 'Operation timed out'. Success still returns success_msg.format(file_name), and all five message templates match the old strings exactly. Failure still returns callback.error with callback.error_code. format() is called on the constant template with file_name as the argument, so braces in a filename are not read as format fields, which matches the old behavior.

Name mangling: _dispatch_command is defined inside ControllerHandler, so self.__controller still resolves to _ControllerHandler__controller. Tests that reach handlers via self.handler._ControllerHandler__handle_action_* (test_controller_handler.py:45,134,795-841) still resolve, because the mangled handler names are kept. Tests that patch ControllerHandler._ACTION_TIMEOUT still work, because _dispatch_command reads self._ACTION_TIMEOUT at call time (line 101).
The new name _dispatch_command has a single underscore, so it is technically overridable by subclasses. No subclass of ControllerHandler exists in src/python, so this has no practical effect.
Performance: no change. There is one extra Python call frame per request, and the blocking wait of up to 30s per request is the same as before.

Blast radius: one module and five HTTP endpoints. If _dispatch_command had a bug, all five single-file actions would fail together, where before each handler was independent. The existing unit tests (queue timeout, delete_local success, traversal rejection for extract/delete_local/delete_remote) exercise both the guarded and unguarded branches of the shared method.
No public API, schema, migration or persisted-data impact.
Verdict: shippable as-is. The behavior is equivalent and no control was lost.

Verified: unquote-then-guard ordering preserved for EXTRACT/DELETE_LOCAL/DELETE_REMOTE (guard=True), QUEUE/STOP correctly omit the guard matching original behavior, all 5 success message templates match originals exactly, self.__controller name-mangling still resolves correctly since _dispatch_command is defined within the same ControllerHandler class, and the new method's parameters are fully type-hinted consistent with the file's convention. No mutable defaults, no bare except, no is/== misuse, no unmanaged resources introduced. The only cosmetic oddity is that _dispatch_command's `action` param uses a quoted forward-reference type hint ("Controller.Command.Action") while _process_bulk_commands's `action` param (line 299, same file) uses the same type unquoted — functionally irrelevant since Controller is already imported at module level, so not reported as a finding (style/taste, not a defect).
